section.title: Performance and thread-safety
section.para: The JAXBContext class is thread safe, but the Marshaller, Unmarshaller, and Validator classes are not thread safe.

For example, suppose you have a multi-thread server application that processes incoming XML documents by &binding.spec.name;. In this case, for the best performance you should have just one instance of JAXBContext in your whole application like this:

example.title: Singleton JAXBContext

section.para: And each time you need to unmarshal/marshal/validate a document. Just create a new Unmarshaller/Marshaller/Validator from this context, like this:

example.title: Thread local Unmarshaller

section.para: This is the simplest safe way to use the &binding.impl.name; from multi-threaded applications.

If you really care about the performance, and/or your application is going to read a lot of small documents, then creating Unmarshaller could be relatively an expensive operation. In that case, consider pooling Unmarshaller objects. Different threads may reuse one Unmarshaller instance, as long as you don't use one instance from two threads at the same time.

section.title: Choosing the XML parser for unmarshalling
section.para: Unmarshaller.unmarshal(InputStream), and likewise the File, URL, Reader, StreamSource and InputSource variants, parse the document with the JAXP SAXParserFactory of the JDK, configured with secure-processing defaults: a DOCTYPE is rejected and external entities are not loaded. On small documents most of the unmarshalling time can be spent setting up and running that parser rather than in &binding.impl.name; itself.

If your application reads many small documents and has a faster StAX implementation such as Woodstox on its classpath, you can create the XMLStreamReader yourself and pass it to Unmarshaller.unmarshal(XMLStreamReader). &binding.impl.name; applies no security settings to a reader it did not create, so configure the factory before using it:

example.title: Unmarshalling through a securely configured StAX reader

listitem.para: Measure with your own documents. The StAX implementation built into the JDK is typically slower than the default SAX path, so this only pays off with a faster provider.
Do not use a StAX factory with its default settings for untrusted input. Woodstox, for example, supports DTDs and external entities by default.

With SUPPORT_DTD disabled, Woodstox skips a DOCTYPE rather than rejecting it: entity references then fail as undeclared, but a document that only contains a DOCTYPE is accepted. If you need such documents rejected, check for XMLStreamConstants.DTD events before unmarshalling.

Setting the javax.xml.parsers.SAXParserFactory system property to a non-Xerces SAX parser does not have the same effect. With secure processing enabled, &binding.impl.name; configures the SAX factory with a Xerces-specific feature, and a parser that does not recognize it makes every unmarshal fail.
